teaser.text: Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust sells a traded share in a managed collection of global growth businesses, including some private companies. Money reaches the trust through investment income, sales, new shares and borrowing, then leaves through costs, debt service, reinvestment, share repurchases and dividends.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust?

paragraphs.text: Portfolio-company growth, margins, customer retention and cash generation decide the case. Private exits and SpaceX sales test carrying values; SpaceX’s weight had fallen to just over 15% at the September Q&A. Debt facilities of US$100 million, US$170 million and US$120 million mature in December 2026, January 2027 and March 2027.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust really make?

paragraphs.text: SMT’s liquidity matters more than a conventional free-cash-flow ratio. Paper gains increase accounting profit, but cash appears only when investments are sold or income is received. In the year to March 2026, investment disposals supplied roughly £2.377 billion, while operating activities consumed £68.721 million.

blocks.heading: What do investors pay for Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust's earnings and cash?

paragraphs.text: A recent factsheet reported a 7.9% discount, while an NAV announcement for 14 October gave a NAV of 1,769.91p. Comparing that NAV with the later market price suggests a discount of about 12.7%, but it is not a verified discount for the same date. Price-to-book is a separate accounting comparison, so it cannot by itself establish a current NAV premium.

P/E is less useful here because investment-trust earnings include gains and losses on investments. In 2026, SMT reported only 2.28p of revenue return but 273.03p of capital return. A rising portfolio can therefore make P/E look unusually low without making the trust a cheap operating business.

blocks.heading: How much does Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust pay per share?

paragraphs.text:
- Baillie Gifford charges 0.30% on the first £4 billion of the specified asset base and 0.25% above that, calculated quarterly.
- Gearing—borrowing used to increase investment exposure—was 11.0% at March 2026; finance costs were £52.695 million.
- The ten largest positions represented 52.45% of total assets at March 2026.
- The 2026 dividend was 4.57p per share against revenue earnings of 2.28p.

blocks.heading: What could change Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust’s dividend?

paragraphs.text: The dividend rounds to £0.05 per share throughout the base case. The bear gives £0.04, while the bull also gives £0.05. The latest payout was 4.57p against revenue earnings of 2.28p, so maintenance depends partly on accumulated income and realised gains rather than current income alone.

blocks.heading: What is Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust’s dividend yield against its price?

paragraphs.text: Borrowing magnifies results slightly and must be paid before shareholders. With £100 of shareholders’ money and £4 borrowed, a 10% asset rise becomes a 10.4% gain before interest, while a fall becomes a 10.4% loss. The small dividend yield means most hoped-for reward must come from capital growth.
